query: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloys are promising bond-coat candidates because of their mechanical properties and elevated-temperature oxidation resistance. Earlier HVAF-M3 work identified 15–45 μm feedstock as optimal for high-quality coatings, but applying the same composition and size range with the HVAF-i7 torch yielded acceptable coating quality yet inadequate thickness. Separate studies of conventional MCrAlY bond coats using the M3 system reported a slight gain in deposition efficiency at higher particle velocity and nozzle-specific best spray distances of 300 and 350 mm. The design target is a sufficiently thick, adherent bond coat that retains coating integrity, minimal as-sprayed oxidation, and durability during high-temperature thermal-barrier service, including deposition within internal diameters as small as 120 mm. What single intervention could overcome the thickness limitation? State the hypothesized intervention and mechanism, predict the outcome relative to the 15–45 μm-feedstock baseline, define the deposition and service conditions under which it should remain effective, identify supporting evidence from the cited prior studies, and propose a controlled experiment with a clear result that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Increasing the particle velocity during HVAF-i7 deposition will enhance the in-flight kinetic energy of the FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy particles, resulting in improved in-flight melting and substrate impact, which overcomes the current thickness limitation while retaining coating integrity and minimal oxidation.
generation.material_initial_state: FeCoNiCrAl high-entropy alloy powders with a feedstock size of 15–45 μm used for HVAF-i7 deposition.
generation.intervention: Adjust the HVAF-i7 process parameters to increase particle velocity (for example, by reducing the optimal nozzle-to-substrate distance toward 300–350 mm and/or increasing propellant flow/pressure) during deposition.
generation.conditions: Deposition should occur within internal diameters as small as 120 mm under high-temperature oxidation service conditions relevant to thermal-barrier applications.
generation.structural_mediator: Enhanced particle kinetic energy leading to improved splatting and in-flight melting, which mediates a better adhesion and a thicker deposit per pass.
generation.mechanism: Higher particle velocity increases the thermal and kinetic impact upon the substrate, which promotes better flattening and splatting of the particles. This effect produces a denser, thicker coating with reduced in-spray oxidation, compensating for the inadequacy seen with the standard HVAF-i7 parameters.
generation.predicted_outcome: A significantly thicker and adherent bond coat is deposited compared to the baseline HVAF-i7 process using the 15–45 μm feedstock, while maintaining minimal oxidation levels and durability during high-temperature service.
generation.baseline: The current HVAF-i7 deposition process with 15–45 μm feedstock yields acceptable coating quality but insufficient thickness.
generation.boundary: The intervention is expected to remain effective provided that the deposition parameters are finely tuned (especially the nozzle-to-substrate distance of approximately 300–350 mm) and the service conditions remain within the elevated-temperature oxidation regime for which the alloy was designed.
generation.uncertainty: It is uncertain whether the HVAF-i7 system can achieve the same level of particle velocity increase as reported in conventional MCrAlY bond coat studies on the M3 system due to potential differences in torch design and spray dynamics; additional system-specific process optimization may be required.

falsification_experiment.design: Conduct a controlled study comparing two sets of HVAF-i7 depositions on FeCoNiCrAl bond coats: one using the baseline particle velocity parameters and another with increased particle velocity achieved by adjusting the nozzle-to-substrate distance (targeting 300–350 mm) and propellant settings. Ensure all other parameters (feedstock size, substrate, ambient conditions) are held constant.
measurements: In-spray oxidation levels (via microstructural analysis and chemical mapping)
Microstructural characterization (to assess splat formation and porosity)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the increased particle velocity condition does not result in a statistically significant improvement in deposit thickness (without sacrificing adhesion and oxidation resistance) relative to the baseline, or if it leads to degradation in coating quality, then the hypothesis will be falsified.

## Abstract
AbstractThis paper considers metallic ultrahigh-temperature materials (UHTMs) and the alloying behaviour and properties of alloys and their phases by using maps of the parameters δ (based on atomic size), Δχ (based on electronegativity), and valence electron concentration (VEC), and discusses what connects and what differentiates material groups in the maps. The formation of high-entropy or complex concentrated intermetallics, namely 5-3 silicides, C14 Laves and A15 compounds, and bcc solid solutions and eutectics in metallic UHTMs and their co-existence with “conventional” phases is discussed. The practicality of maps for the design/selection of substrate alloys is deliberated upon. The need for environmental coatings for metallic UHTMs was considered and the design of bond coat alloys is discussed by using relevant maps.Keywords: high-entropy alloys, complex concentrated alloys, refractory metal intermetallic composites, high-entropy intermetallics, complex concentrated intermetallics, alloy design
